caption: Riley's major Weber citing acts: object, move, stance, and analytical job

cells.value: Privilege and Property (2003)
"Class, Status, Party," From Max Weber (Weber 1946:194)

anchor.quote: Following in this Gramscian and Weberian tradition, the central theoretical point of this paper is to show how the structure of political society matters for group formation.

cells.value: Genealogy / self-positioning
Builds on
Establishes political society as irreducible to state or civil society; Gramscian institutions carry the empirical mechanism
Civic Associations and Authoritarian Regimes (2005)
Methodology of the Social Sciences (Weber 1949:172)

anchor.quote: an analysis of suppressed alternatives embedded in historical sequences (Moore 1978:385–91; Weber 1949:172)

cells.value: Authority (methodological cluster)
Builds on

Tony Judt: A Cooler Look (2011)
"Politics as a Vocation," ethic of responsibility

anchor.quote: Both Sartre and Weber refused the comfortable stance of the moralizer because they were aware of the tension between ethics and politics

cells.value: Authority / dialogue (corrective)
Builds on
Replaces Judt's detached moralism with responsibility for political violence; pairs Weber with Sartre as honest confronters of the ethics–politics tension
Routes or Rivals? (2013)
Economy and Society, p. 919 (imperialist capitalism prognosis)

anchor.quote: It is true that Weber insisted that inter-state competition was saturated with conflicts over prestige. But he also argued that there was a strong material dynamic to imperialism.

cells.value: Evidence / dialogue (corrective of Mann)
Adopts provisionally
Adds a material dynamic to prestige conflict; corrects Mann's ideological-militarism account; middle stage of political-capitalism trajectory
What Is Trump? (2018)
Economy and Society, pp. 1028–31 (patrimonial and bureaucratic domination)

anchor.quote: Here it may be useful to recall Weber's three forms of rule, each with its own apparatus of domination and logic of legitimation: the charismatic, the patrimonial and the bureaucratic.

cells.value: Authority / evidence (applied typology)
Builds on and qualifies
Diagnoses Trump as patrimonial misfit inside a legal-rational state; rejects fascism analogy; patrimonialism is pre-modern type inserted as foreign body
Faultlines (2020)
Economy and Society, p. 917 (Roman imperialist capitalism)

anchor.quote: Adapting Weber's concept of Roman 'imperialist capitalism', this could perhaps be termed 'political capitalism'

cells.value: Dialogue / declared adaptation
Adapts
Names contemporary profit secured through direct political power; marks the conceptual transfer explicitly as adaptation, not identity
Science and Politics: Reflections on Wendy Brown (2023)
Vocation lectures; fact/value distinction

anchor.quote: Weber illicitly extended his problem, which was the ultimate non-justifiability of nationalism as a value, to values in general.

cells.value: Foil / selective reconstruction
Builds on and qualifies
Historicises Weber's fact/value sundering as German nationalist politics; retains responsibility and objective possibilities while rejecting the generalised value-pluralism
Relational Power Theory (2024, with Emigh)
Economy and Society: power definition (p. 53), domination, bureaucracy, legitimacy

anchor.quote: Weber (1921/1978, p. 53) defined power as "the probability that one actor within a social relationship will be in a position to carry out his own will despite resistance"

cells.value: Authority / evidence (component supply)
Builds on and qualifies
Supplies components (domination, legitimacy, information asymmetry) for a relational power theory; Marx provides exploitation, Gramsci hegemony, Weber organisation
The Rise of Political Capitalism (2025)
Weber 1922, p. 180 (estate / Stand, MWG I/23)

anchor.quote: When workers organise in this second way they do not form a class, they form what Max Weber called an "estate" (Weber 1922, p. 180).

cells.value: Authority (categorical distinction)
Adopts
Distinguishes materially grounded closure from class formation; inserts estate into a Marxian theory of market interests and exploitation
The Long Downturn and Its Political Results (2025, with Brenner)
Economy and Society, pp. 965–66 (tax-farming, political capitalism origin)

anchor.quote: The origins of the term are to be sought in Max Weber, Gabriel Kolko and Murray Rothbard.

cells.value: Genealogy / historical analogy
Builds on
Reconstructs tax-farming as historical archetype of politically constituted rent; distinguishes modern asset-price mechanism from direct fiscal extraction
Angles of Vision (2026)
Weber's analysis of capitalism (no specific work cited)

anchor.quote: Marx approached capitalism from the standpoint of wage labour, Weber from that of the owners of capital.

cells.value: Foil / dialogue (standpoint contrast)
Builds on and contains
Credits Weber's firm-centred standpoint as highly revealing while subordinating it to a Lukácsian Marxist synthesis privileging the wage-labour perspective
First Principles (2026)
Weber on market-differentiated class positions (no locus cited)

anchor.quote: the class is fundamentally fractured by the material interests deriving from the market position of its component parts as Weber noted long ago.

cells.value: Authority (methodological)
Adopts
Grounds the claim that worker interests diverge materially within wage labour; suturing those interests to class-wide solidarity is Riley's Gramscian addition

note: Early texts (2003–2005) place Weber alongside Gramsci as methodological or genealogical authority; middle texts (2011–2020) apply typologies directly (responsibility, patrimonialism, political capitalism) and mark adaptations explicitly; late texts (2022–2026) either systematise (estate politics, tax-farming genealogy) or contain Weber within a Lukácsian standpoint critique, with the Gramscian-Marxian framework consistently carrying the explanatory core.
proves: Across twelve major citing acts spanning 2003–2026, Riley treats Weber as a modular interlocutor whose distinctions are borrowed selectively and progressively subordinated to a Gramscian-Marxian account of exploitation, accumulation, and class formation.

caption: Checked Riley–Weber citation pairs: attribution, verdict, and Weber witness

cells.value: RW0001 — political society formula (2003)
Political society is reducible neither to civil-society interests nor to the state

anchor.quote: Following in this Gramscian and Weberian tradition, the central theoretical point of this paper is to show how the structure of political society matters for group formation.

cells.value: Selective
Weber's "Class, Status, Party" differentiates economic, social, and power orders but does not state Riley's full mediating-domain formula
Parties live in a house of power — spheres are differentiated, not fused into Riley's political-society filter
RW0002–0003 — suppressed alternatives (2005)
Historical sequences contain suppressed alternatives; intrinsic possibilities establish causal importance

anchor.quote: an analysis of suppressed alternatives embedded in historical sequences (Moore 1978:385–91; Weber 1949:172)

cells.value: Unverifiable
Retrieval reached German MWG editorial matter and Roscher discussion rather than the cited English Methodology p. 172; no edition equivalence established
No Weber witness recovered at the cited locus
RW0011 — ethic of responsibility (2011)
Political actors accept responsibility for violence and foreseeable consequences; conviction and responsibility are supplements

anchor.quote: An ethic of conviction and an ethic of responsibility were not 'absolute contrasts, but rather supplements'.

cells.value: Fair
Weber requires an account of foreseeable results and acknowledges morally dangerous political means; the "supplements" clause is supported though the routed window stops short of the exact page
Weber: an ethic of responsibility requires giving an account of the foreseeable results of one's action — witness supports the substantive contrast
RW0016 — imperialism prognosis (2013)
Imperialist capitalism and political expansion are predictably recurrent

anchor.quote: It is true that Weber insisted that inter-state competition was saturated with conflicts over prestige. But he also argued that there was a strong material dynamic to imperialism.

cells.value: Accurate
Riley's quotation of Weber's prognosis matches the retrieved passage word for word

anchor.quote: For the predictable future, the prognosis will have to be made in its favor

cells.value: RW0023 — state definition in census article (2015)
Weber defines the state through bureaucratic and infrastructural capacities

anchor.quote: It deploys Weber's (1958: 77–78) definition of the state in terms of organizational means—its bureaucratic and infrastructural capacities.

cells.value: Stretched
The cited pages define the modern state through its successful claim to monopoly of legitimate physical force within a territory — not infrastructural capacity
Weber at pp. 77–78: a state is a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory
RW0029 — capitalism–suffrage thesis (2015)
Weber alone grasped the deep affinity between industrial capitalism, mass suffrage, and a strengthened representative state

anchor.quote: Only Weber understood the deep affinity between modern industrial capitalism and mass suffrage

cells.value: Selective
The retrieved pages defend parliament through consent, accountability, and leadership functions but do not state the complete capitalism–suffrage affinity proposition
Weber: parliaments are today the means of manifesting the minimum consent — parliamentary function is supported; the full affinity synthesis exceeds the locus
RW0042 — patrimonial office (2018)
Patrimonial office lacks public/private separation and rests on personal loyalty

anchor.quote: The patrimonial office lacks above all the bureaucratic separation of the 'private' and the 'official' sphere.

cells.value: Accurate
Both predicates — absence of private/official separation and personal loyalty — occur at the cited pages in Economy and Society
Weber at pp. 1028–31: the patrimonial office lacks above all the bureaucratic separation of the private and the official sphere — exact match
RW0045 — Roman imperialist capitalism adaptation (2020)
Weber's Roman imperialist capitalism = profit through direct political power; adapted to contemporary political capitalism

anchor.quote: Adapting Weber's concept of Roman 'imperialist capitalism', this could perhaps be termed 'political capitalism'

cells.value: Fair
Riley declares the adaptation explicitly and retains Weber's mechanism of profit through direct exploitation of political power directed toward expansion
Weber at p. 917: the profit opportunities of all these groups rest upon the direct exploitation of political power directed towards expansion
RW0048–0049 — rationalization and positivism (2021)
Weber's rationalization account (E&S 86–93) links capitalism to positivism; General Economic History 275–77 extends this

anchor.quote: Externalist theory correctly suggests that methodological positivism is associated with the rise of industrial capitalism.

cells.value: Unverifiable
Retrieved E&S pages discuss calculability and formal rationality; positivism is absent from the window; the General Economic History locus is unheld
No witness recovered that connects the cited Weber pages to the positivism attribution
RW0050 — life-conduct question (2021)
Weber asks what we should do and how to arrange our lives, a question science cannot answer

anchor.quote: most were eager to provide an answer to Weber's (1946: 152–53) query: "What shall we do, and, how shall we arrange our lives?"

cells.value: Accurate
The question appears in Weber's discussion of what science cannot answer; Riley preserves the scientific limit
Weber in Science as a Vocation: science does not answer the question — what shall we — the witness supports the attribution exactly
RW0064 — Machiavellian example (2023)
Weber's called politician exemplified by Florentine citizens who placed civic greatness above salvation

anchor.quote: Weber instances as the most compelling example of the "called" politician "those citizens"

cells.value: Accurate
Weber invokes the Florentine citizens at the cited page while discussing the tension between political means and salvation ethics
Weber at p. 126: Machiavelli praises those citizens who deemed the greatness of their native city higher than the salvation of their souls
RW0074 — legitimacy / political formula analogy (2024)
Weberian legitimacy is analogous to Mosca's political formula

anchor.quote: The role of the political formula is somewhat analogous to Weber's (1921, p. 398) concept of legitimacy

cells.value: Unverifiable
Cited German Gesammelte politische Schriften p. 398 is unheld; retrieved English window is editorial matter from another collection
No Weber witness recovered at the cited locus
RW0076 — power definition (2024)
Power is the probability an actor carries out its will despite resistance

anchor.quote: Weber (1921/1978, p. 53) defined power as "the probability that one actor within a social relationship will be in a position to carry out his own will despite resistance"

cells.value: Accurate
Riley's quotation matches Weber's definition at the cited page word for word
Weber at E&S p. 53: a Power (Macht) is the probability that one actor within a social relationship will be in a position to carry out his own will despite resistance
RW0077–0080 — power-holder polarities (2024)
Power can be held by people; may be formal or informal; varies between cooperation and conflict; rests on material and other resources

anchor.quote: Power can be held by people (Weber, 1921/1978, pp. 954, 1112)

cells.value: Unverifiable

Retrieved pages treat legitimacy, charisma, and patriarchalism; none states the formal/informal polarity, the cooperative/conflictual continuum, or the people-as-power-holders proposition in the attributed form
No witness recovered that carries the complete attributed predicates at the cited pages
RW0081 — organizational domination (2024)
Organizations work primarily through domination, not resource control as such

anchor.quote: But organizations primarily work through domination, not through the control of resources as such

cells.value: Fair
Weber's E&S confirms that economic organizations exhibit structures of domination and that bureaucracy is technically superior; the sharper command/ownership contrast is the authors' synthesis
Weber: the great majority of all economic organizations exhibit domination structures — the core claim holds; the synthesis exceeds the locus
RW0082 — lower-level information dependence (2024)
Leadership depends on information embedded in lower levels of the organization

anchor.quote: the leadership often depends on information embedded in lower levels of the organization that can be hard to extract

cells.value: Selective
Weber treats official information as a bureaucratic advantage over parliamentary supervisors; Riley redirects this into a general elite-dependence-on-subordinates thesis
Weber: the bureaucrat has official information which is only available through administrative channels — immediate object is bureaucratic power over parliament, not general downward dependence
RW0084 — legitimacy qualification (2024)
Following any authority at least in part depends on belief in its legitimacy

anchor.quote: following any authority at least in part depends on the belief in its legitimacy

cells.value: Accurate
Weber states that domination normally cultivates belief in legitimacy alongside other motives; the "at least in part" qualification preserves Weber's additional compliance motives
Weber: every such system attempts to establish and cultivate the belief in its legitimacy — qualification preserved
RW0085 — estate application (2025)
Workers organized through race, ethnicity, or credentials form an estate rather than a class

anchor.quote: When workers organise in this second way they do not form a class, they form what Max Weber called an "estate" (Weber 1922, p. 180).

cells.value: Fair
Riley preserves class/estate nonidentity and material grounding but compresses Weber's criteria of special esteem, life conduct, and effective monopoly
Weber at MWG I/23 marginal A180: Stand defined by effective special esteem and possible monopolies within an association — compression confirmed
RW0088 — tax-farming genealogy (2025)
Weber is an origin of political capitalism; tax-farming is its archetypal historical manifestation

anchor.quote: The origins of the term are to be sought in Max Weber, Gabriel Kolko and Murray Rothbard.

cells.value: Selective
E&S pp. 965–66 explains the tax-farming mechanism but does not itself use the term political capitalism or establish Weber's terminological priority
Weber at pp. 965–66: farming out public tax collection in lieu of the lord's own management served this purpose — mechanism confirmed; nomenclature and priority are not
RW0096 — broad political-capitalism definition (date unknown)
Weber defined political capitalism as profit-oriented activity relying predominantly on political rather than productivity-enhancing means

anchor.quote: The term was originally deployed by Max Weber to describe economic activity that is profit-oriented but relies predominantly on political means

cells.value: Selective
The cited pages (E&S 965–66) establish tax-farming and power-based acquisition but do not state the broad contrast between political means and productivity-enhancing investment as a definition
Weber at pp. 965–66: enterprises based on capital accounting may be oriented toward power-based acquisition — partial support; the full definitional contrast exceeds the locus

note: Direct quotations and narrow definitions (RW0016, RW0042, RW0050, RW0064, RW0076, RW0084) consistently hold; declared adaptations (RW0045, RW0085) remain fair when the transformation is explicit; selective enlargement occurs when a local passage is made to carry a wider synthesis (RW0001, RW0029, RW0082, RW0088, RW0096); the census article's state definition (RW0023) is the sole stretched verdict; twelve pairs remain unverifiable due to retrieval failure, edition mismatch, or absent predicate.
proves: Fidelity varies systematically by citation type: narrow quotations and declared adaptations are generally accurate or fair, while synthetic attributions that make a local Weber passage carry a broader theoretical claim are selective or, in one case, stretched.

caption: Riley and supplied Weber readers positioned on three fault-line themes

cells.value: Riley, 2003 and 2025
Estate politics and class formation

anchor.quote: This system did not allow class interests to be translated into political claims.

cells.value: 2003: privilege-based status blocks class formation; 2025: workers organizing through race or credentials form estates, not classes
Internal trajectory — 2003 uses status to explain historical failure of class; 2025 generalises to contemporary labour under political capitalism
Riley, 2018
Estate concepts applied to advanced capitalism

anchor.quote: the Bourdieusean research program is mistaken because it applies a conceptual apparatus appropriate to pre-capitalist social formations

cells.value: Rejects applying estate-type analysis to advanced capitalism as a category error
Stands in unresolved tension with Riley 2025, which applies estate politics to advanced political capitalism — the reconciliation is not performed in the supplied texts
Riley, 2025
Estate politics under political capitalism

anchor.quote: political struggles are likely to unfold in such a way that they re-enforce estate-type politics rather than class politics

cells.value: Political capitalism structurally reinforces estate-type defensive struggles among wage earners
Self-relation: revises or contradicts the 2018 rejection; the supplied texts do not explicitly reconcile the two positions
Erik Olin Wright, 2002
Estate politics and class formation

anchor.quote: both saw capitalism as systematically eroding the salience of traditional status groups.

cells.value: Capitalism systematically erodes traditional status groups; status affects welfare indirectly through coercive exclusion mechanisms
Consonant with Riley on material basis of closure; contrasts with Riley 2025 — where Wright predicts erosion, Riley predicts reinforcement of estates under political capitalism
Erik Olin Wright, 2002
Weber's market-centred class analysis vs. Marxist exploitation

anchor.quote: the Weberian account revolves exclusively around market transactions, whereas the Marxist account also emphasizes the

cells.value: Weber centres market life chances and technical rationality, marginalising exploitation and worker resistance; this aligns Weberian class analysis with capitalist interests
Consonant with Riley's 2026 owner/firm standpoint diagnosis; Wright does not cite Riley — analytical convergence without demonstrated influence
Venelin Ganev, 2009
Political capitalism: causal route

anchor.quote: political capitalism emerges from social and institutional disarray

cells.value: Political capitalism = institutional disintegration, de-bureaucratisation, and privilege over rights — not coherent state tutelage; rational acquisition and political capitalism must be cast as contrasting categories

Consonant with Riley on categorical distinction between market profit and political extraction; divergent on mechanism — Ganev: state weakness and disarray; Riley 2020–2025: systematic state support for asset prices
Venelin Ganev, 2009
Corruption and governance under political capitalism

anchor.quote: Corrupt practices are not a style of governing - they are an assault on the infrastructure of governance.

cells.value: Postcommunist political capitalism is privilege-centred, not rights-centred; corruption destroys governance infrastructure rather than governing through it
Affinity with Riley's early privilege-based closure analysis; diverges from Riley's later account in which politically engineered asset inflation presupposes capable fiscal and monetary agencies
Riley, 2013 and 2020
Political capitalism: trajectory across texts

anchor.quote: Adapting Weber's concept of Roman 'imperialist capitalism', this could perhaps be termed 'political capitalism'

cells.value: 2013: Weber corrects Mann — imperialism has a material dynamic alongside prestige; 2020: explicit adaptation of Roman imperialist capitalism to contemporary profit through political power
Internal development — moves from Weber as corrective evidence to Weber as named source for an adapted category
Riley and Brenner, 2025
Political capitalism: modern mechanism vs. historical archetype

anchor.quote: Today, however, the key mechanism structuring this rent is not so much the direct privatization of the state's fiscal functions

cells.value: Contemporary political capitalism operates through asset-price support, not direct fiscal privatisation; tax-farming is historical archetype, not current mechanism
Distinguishes Riley's modern theory from Ganev's postcommunist case and from the historical Weber locus — a differentiation internal to Riley's own trajectory
Riley, 2023
Fact–value distinction: historicisation

anchor.quote: his sundering of "fact" and "value" (a sundering that Brown rightly describes as a police action), was a political move

cells.value: Weber's fact/value sundering was a historically specific political intervention against Marxist scientific socialism and German nationalism, not a timeless philosophical solution
Self-position — more critical than Riley's 2011 orthodox adoption of responsibility; contrasts with Ktenas and Bendix who defend Wertfreiheit as a genuine methodological achievement
Yannis Ktenas, 2021
Fact–value distinction: Wertfreiheit and standpoint

anchor.quote: The person who speaks from this Gesichtspunkt certainly plays an active and creative role in the process of knowledge

cells.value: Wertfreiheit presupposes rather than excludes value-laden standpoints; situated inquiry is active and creative but not arbitrary; Weber traced tendencies and chances, not strict determinisms
Consonant with Riley's achieved-standpoint account of the Marx/Weber contrast; contrasts with Riley's claim that Weber's generalised value-pluralism was an illicit nationalist extension
Reinhard Bendix, 1960
Fact–value distinction: passionate impartiality

anchor.quote: Committed as few others were to the exclusion of political value judgments from academic teaching

cells.value: Weber's exclusion of political value judgments from academic teaching is compatible with passionate partisanship for impartiality and substantive political commitment outside the lecture hall
Consonant with Riley's rejection of value-free indifference; less critical — Bendix defends the distinction as compatible with commitment, whereas Riley historicises it as ideologically motivated
Riley, 2026 (Angles of Vision)
Marx/Weber standpoint contrast

anchor.quote: Marx approached capitalism from the standpoint of wage labour, Weber from that of the owners of capital.

cells.value: Weber's angle of vision is the firm and owners of capital — highly revealing but limited to what is visible from that perspective; Marx's wage-labour standpoint discloses capitalism as a class structure
Self-position — endorses Lukácsian Einkesselung of Weber; consonant with Wright's exploitation critique; more epistemologically explicit than any earlier Riley text
John Rundell, 2014
Patrimonialism and political organisation

anchor.quote: Urban rulership also became increasingly autonomous, that is was instituted outside the orbit of the patrimonial state.

cells.value: Autonomous medieval city exists outside the patrimonial state; political power circulates between closure and opening; groups figurate the political from positions of closure or circumscription

Consonant with Riley's institutional pluralism and use of patrimonial/non-patrimonial contrast; different substantive object (medieval democratic fragility vs. contemporary Trumpian rule); no demonstrated engagement
Ktenas, 2021 / Riley, 2018 and 2023
Anti-speculative history vs. hidden dogmatism

anchor.quote: Weber traced tendencies and chances but not strict determinisms in the field of human action.

cells.value: Ktenas: Weber's anti-speculative stance is a genuine achievement — oriented to tendencies and chances, not fixed determination; Riley: Weberian preference for partial theories is a hidden dogmatism

anchor.quote: Isn't their scepticism just a hidden dogmatism?

cells.value: John R. Love, 1991
Political capitalism and tax-farming in antiquity

anchor.quote: We must therefore conclude that Weber's use of the term capitalism is not consistent.

cells.value: Weber's ancient-capitalism concept oscillates between incompatible criteria; tax-farming does not satisfy a market-exchange definition of capitalism

Interpretive contrast — Love's internal critique of Weber challenges the stable Weberian anchor that Riley and Brenner invoke for their tax-farming genealogy; Love predates Riley's texts and does not cite him
Reinhard Bendix, 1960
Continuity of Weber's empirical and conceptual work

anchor.quote: contain in rudimentary form the basic concepts and central problems which occupied him for the rest of his life.

cells.value: Weber's early empirical studies are the route to his intellectual unity; the later central concepts grow from his historical practice rather than from isolated methodological formulations
Methodologically consonant with Riley's historically specific applications of Weber; Bendix predates Riley's supplied works — no direct engagement possible

note: On estate politics the three-way tension among Riley 2003, Wright 2002, and Riley 2025 is unresolved — the later reinforcement of estates contradicts both Wright's erosion prediction and Riley's own 2018 rejection of estate concepts for advanced capitalism; on political capitalism Ganev and Riley are consonant on categorical distinctiveness but divergent on causal mechanism (disarray vs. systematic state support); on fact–value Riley's historicist critique contrasts with Ktenas's and Bendix's defences of Wertfreiheit as compatible with situated commitment.
proves: Riley is selectively consonant with the supplied Weber readers on categorical distinctions but revisionist on three fault lines — estate politics under advanced capitalism, the causal route of political capitalism, and the fact-value problem — none of which has been resolved in the supplied texts.
